passages.text: The question: How should humans behave and organise themselves? Can science alone, or religion alone, define correct ethical behaviour and the right form of society?

This study examines behaviour, ethics, and social organisation in Madhyasth Darshan (Co-existentialism), as presented by Shri A. Nagraj, and compares its answers with physics and the natural sciences, Advaita Vedanta, and selected religious and technocratic approaches to human conduct and social order.
Dotted underline: definition · Blue underline: link

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: Standpoint and scope

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: These studies are written from the standpoint of a scientist and technologist — someone trained to graduate-level physics and mathematics, at home with contemporary cosmology, quantum theory, conservation laws, and the logic of formal models.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: From that background, a familiar picture of nature is hard to avoid: consciousness appears as something the brain does — an epiphenomenon, functional outcome, or emergent property of particular configurations of very large numbers of physical particles. Modern physics and cognitive science are powerful on mechanism, prediction, and public evidence; yet the hard problem of consciousness, the status of the self, and the reality of value remain fiercely contested. The standpoint taken here does not treat those gaps as settled in favour of matter-only reductionism.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: The work begins where that scientific picture leaves open questions — and asks whether Madhyasth Darshan offers a coherent alternative worth examining seriously. This paper reads the primary texts carefully, states what follows from the darshan itself, and compares it in parallel with what we know from physics and the natural sciences, Advaita Vedanta, and modern Western philosophy (especially moral science and social philosophy). Physics and mathematics are one leg of that comparison, not the only one. The aim is rigorous comparative understanding — testing definitions, internal consistency, and fit with public knowledge — not persuasion or devotional endorsement.

passages.heading: standpoint-and-scope
passages.text: These topical studies state the philosophy in clear, checkable prose first. A separate formal mathematical treatment may follow once the definitions and relations are stable across the studies; this paper does not assume or require that treatment.

passages.heading: quick-glossary
passages.text: Quick Glossary

passages.heading: quick-glossary
passages.text: Term Plain meaning Jeevan The sentient self — a real unit that works through the body; for ontology see The Ontology of Coexistence. Knowledge order (gyan avastha) The human level of nature — able to know and evaluate every other level. Dharma Orderliness; in conduct, living in line with resolved understanding of existence. Right-use (sadupyog) Use of body, mind, and resources that serves humane purpose, not mere appetite or profit. Undivided society Social order that moves beyond sectarian or defensive groupings toward universal human orderliness. MVD / SB / JV Primary Madhyasth Darshan texts cited in this study; full bibliographic entries under References.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1. The Madhyasth Darshan answer

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan holds that humans should behave as awakened knowledge-order beings, not merely as instinct-driven animals, profit-seeking consumers, or rule-following religious subjects. They should organise themselves through families, communities, undivided society, and universal orderliness, grounded in coexistence, justice, resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and humane conduct. The darshan does not treat ethics as arbitrary moral instruction; it derives behaviour from a larger ontology in which existence is coexistence, all orders of nature are complementary, and humans are the order capable of knowing this and living accordingly.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.1 Core assumptions

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The behavioural argument rests on a chain of premises, from coexistence to practical conduct:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: # Assumption Why it matters 1 Existence is coexistence. Reality is not fundamentally conflict, domination, or isolated self-interest. Ethics must be based on complementarity, not competition or negation. 2 Existence is orderly. Orderliness is already present in nature; humans are the order in which it is not yet fully evidenced. Human society should become orderly by understanding existence, not by coercion alone. 3 Humans are knowledge-order beings. Humans alone can know the properties, nature, and dharma of all orders. Human behaviour must be guided by understanding, not merely instinct, fear, or commandment. 4 Every human seeks satisfaction, happiness, and restfulness. Even deluded behaviour is an attempt to solve suffering. Ethics is not external punishment; it is the correct route to fulfilment. 5 The root human problem is delusion. Humans mistake partial satisfactions for complete fulfilment and confuse body-needs with jeevan-needs. Social disorder is a symptom of wrong understanding. 6 Humane conduct is studyable and livable. It is not merely a sermon or private mystical state. Behaviour can be taught, learned, verified, and embodied. 7 Relationships contain values. Sociality means fulfilling values inherent in relationships and contacts. Society is not just a contract or herd; it is value-fulfilment in mutuality. 8 Resolution and prosperity are both required. Thought must be resolved; material life must be adequately provided for. Ethics cannot be only spiritual renunciation or only material production. 9 Organisation requires shared cause, goal, and programme. Families, communities, and society need a common purpose to remain coherent. 10 Coercive power and religious command have failed to produce universal ethical conduct. Neither state-force nor religious law is sufficient without understanding.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.2 What is the human purpose?

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD explicitly states that human life is directed toward restfulness:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Humans on this Earth are engaged in endeavours and experiments to know and recognise their significance, solely for attaining restfulness.” - MVD, Ch. 4, The Human Purpose

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The progression is not from individual desire to social contract, but from sociality to need, production, right-use, humane conduct, and undivided sociality:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Sociality gives rise to needs; needs give rise to experimentation and production; experimentation and production give rise to creation of wealth; creation of wealth gives rise to use, right-use and purposeful-use; use, right-use and purposeful-use give rise to practicality; practicality gives rise to humaneness, and humaneness gives rise to sociality. Sociality is meaningful when it is towards undivided sociality.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Wealth and production are not rejected in this chain; they are subordinated to:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: use (upyog)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: right-use (sadupyog)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: purposeful-use (prayojansheelta)

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: humane conduct

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: undivided society

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3 How should humans behave?

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD classifies human tendencies into three broad categories:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Based on the above, human tendencies is seen to have three categories: (1) Inhumaneness, (2) Humaneness and (3) Higher humaneness.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.1 Inhumaneness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Inhuman behaviour is defined by nature, propensities, and perspectives:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Servility, perfidy and cruelty itself is inhumane nature.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Eating, sleeping, defending and mating are the inhumane propensities.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Pleasant-unpleasant, healthy-unhealthy and profit-loss only are the inhumane perspectives.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This does not mean food, sleep, health, and livelihood are bad. It means that if behaviour is governed only by these, humans remain below their knowledge-order potential.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.2 Humaneness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Humane behaviour is defined by higher nature and higher perspective:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Fortitude, courage, and generosity itself is humane nature.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Justice-injustice, dharma-adharma, and truth-untruth are humane perspectives.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: So human behaviour should be guided by:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: justice, not merely liking/disliking

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: dharma/orderliness, not merely bodily benefit

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: truth, not merely profit

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.3 Higher-humaneness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Higher-humaneness is defined as:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Kindness, grace and compassion itself is the higher-humane nature.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This moves behaviour from mere justice toward active benevolence: helping others gain both the content and receptivity required for awakening.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.4 Values in relationships

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD defines sociality as value-fulfilment:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Fulfilling the values inherent in relationships and contacts itself is sociality.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: SB similarly says complementarity is realised through relationships:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “For humans, this complementary way is realised through recognising and fulfilling relationships. It is evident, and can be studied, that wherever humans recognise relationships, the fulfilment of values is also observed.” - SB, Resolution by Way of Complementarity

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The primary ethical unit is not the isolated individual, nor the state, nor the religious community. It is the human-in-relationship.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Correct behaviour means:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: recognise relationships

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: understand expectations within them

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: fulfil values such as trust, affection, respect, care, guidance, and responsibility

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: avoid betrayal, deceit, exploitation, violence, and retaliation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.5 Justice, not merely legality

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD defines justice as orderliness of behaviour that protects humaneness:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Justice pertains to the orderliness of behaviour based on policies that protect humaneness.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: It also says:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The necessary behaviour for humans is to adhere to the laws of justice, and the necessary thought for humans is to adhere to the laws of dharma.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This is a significant distinction. Law is not enough. A behaviour may be legal and still not humane if it violates justice, relationship, trust, or coexistence.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.6 Resolution and prosperity together

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD says sociality needs both intellectual and material fulfilment:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Intellectual resolution is achieved through intellectual exercise and endeavour, while material prosperity is achieved through physical experimentation, endeavour, and production. Both intellectual resolution and material prosperity are helpful for the development of sociality.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This rejects two common extremes:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: materialism: production and wealth are enough

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: renunciation-only spirituality: material prosperity is irrelevant

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan says humans need:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: resolution in understanding

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: prosperity in family/material life

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: fearlessness in society

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: coexistence with nature

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.3.7 Complementarity toward nature

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: SB states:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “Every order in existence has its respective use, right-use, and purpose, inherently bonded by the natural way of existence. This is the way of complementarity.” - SB, Resolution by Way of Complementarity

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: It criticises modern human conduct:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “For humans, it is evident that the material, biological, and animal orders are mutually complementary. They exist in harmony with each other and are complementary for humans. However, by the end of the twentieth century, the actions of humans have demonstrated the opposite: instead of being complementary to the nature of the other three orders, humans have acted in opposition and revolt.” - SB

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: JV makes the ecological point more sharply:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The big benefit from this understanding will be that humans shall live on this Earth forever - without wounding it, without tearing its guts apart, and without destroying it.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: So human behaviour toward Earth should not be extraction, conquest, or unlimited consumption. It should be right-use of natural abundance.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4 How should humans organise themselves?

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan treats organisation as the social expression of resolved understanding — from shared purpose through family and community to undivided society.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4.1 Shared cause, goal, and programme

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD states:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “For an organisation, commonness of cause and goal is necessary. For its sustainment, commonness of the program is also necessary.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This means a society cannot be stable merely by force, market exchange, shared identity, or ritual. It needs:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: shared understanding of why it exists

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: shared aim

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: shared practical programme

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4.2 The progression of organisation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD defines human groupings:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “More than one human coming together or becoming organised is referred to as a family, community, or undivided society. In the awakened human tradition, undivided society is evidenced along with the universal orderliness.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: The intended progression runs from person through family and community to undivided society and universal orderliness. The decisive point is that the family or community must not remain sectarian, defensive, or identity-bound; it must move toward undivided society.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4.3 Family-based self-organising orderliness

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD defines higher-humane social order:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “A higher-humanely societal orderliness is exemplified by undivided society, family-based self-organising orderliness, as evidence of humane tradition.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: This suggests that the family is not treated merely as a private emotional unit. It is the first school of:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: production

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: relationship

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: duty

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: responsibility

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: education

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: value fulfilment

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: social participation

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: But this depends on a wise family, not any family as it happens to exist. The family must be aligned with justice, right-use, and sociality.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4.4 Resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD distinguishes animal collectivity from awakened human sociality:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The semblance of collectivity among animals is generally observed only in situations of fear. Under no circumstances is such collectivity observed in activities of study, production, or the maintenance of orderliness. In contrast, the foundational basis of sociality in awakened humans is living in resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Awakened sociality means living in resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence — not the fear-bound collectivity animals sometimes show.

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: 1.4.5 From selfishness to benevolence

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: MVD distinguishes resource-use by intention:

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The planning to utilise resources in a limited and narrow way confined only to one person or family is referred to as selfishness. It signifies thoughts and behaviours aimed at seeking sensory pleasure and comfort only for oneself or one’s family.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The thoughts and behaviours directed towards the comfort of others along with prioritisation of utilising resources for this purpose are referred to as altruism.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: “The thoughts and behaviours that accomplish universal wellbeing along with resolution, offer solutions to problems, foster relationships based purely on affection, and utilise resources to make these accessible to all are referred to as benevolent.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 1-the-madhyasth-darshan-answer
passages.text: Selfish use confines resources to one person or family; altruistic use extends comfort to others; benevolent use aims at universal wellbeing through resolution, problem-solving, affectionate relationships, and shared access to resources. The highest organisation is not merely welfare or charity, but making resolution and humane living available to all.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Mainstream science and technocracy are powerful on observation, production, and modelling means, but science alone cannot define correct human behaviour in Madhyasth Darshan’s reading, because science as commonly practised is seen as:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: matter-centric

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: instrument-centric

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: often mechanistic about humans

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: good at means, weak at ends

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: capable of production but not necessarily resolution

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: JV criticises reliance on science to fix human disorder:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “We humans committed all these crimes during the scientific age, yet we haven’t stopped boasting about science! We think science will find a lasting solution to this situation, even though the human race is on the verge of being wiped out from Earth.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: It also criticises power-centric constitutions:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “Power-Centric Rule gets implemented in the form of three activities - stopping one mistake by making another mistake, stopping one crime by committing another crime, and stopping one war by waging another war. Yet there is no evidence anywhere if these three actions could rid us of crimes.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The critique is not that science is useless. Science is accepted as useful for observation, production, and understanding physical processes. The critique is that science alone cannot determine humane ends:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: what is justice?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: what is right-use?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: what is human fulfilment?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: what is a proper relationship?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: what level of consumption is enough?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: why should humans choose coexistence over domination?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Science can describe consequences, but it does not by itself generate a complete normative order.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1 Is human order just an optimization problem?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: A modern scientific or technocratic view may say:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Humans and organisations are systems that optimise. We only need to find the right parameters - survival, health, pleasure, happiness, productivity, cooperation, social stability - and then organise behaviour to maximise them.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan would treat this as insufficient, not because parameters are useless, but because the choice of parameter already depends on a view of the human being. If the human is treated as only body, animal, consumer, or machine, the parameters will be chosen from that level: survival, comfort, pleasure, security, efficiency, profit, or measurable happiness. Those parameters do not reach the full human purpose.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: MVD gives a direct framework for this critique through the six perspectives of behaviour:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “All human behaviour is manifest in six perspectives: - (1) pleasant-unpleasant, (2) healthy-unhealthy, (3) profit-loss, (4) justice-injustice, (5) dharma-adharma, and (6) truth-untruth.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: It then separates inhumane and humane behaviour:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “The behaviour of humans with inhumane perspective is in the refuge of pleasant-unpleasant, healthy-unhealthy, and profit-loss. The behaviour of humans with humane perspective is in the refuge of justice-injustice, dharma-adharma, and truth-untruth.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: This is the key answer to the optimization view. Survival and physical health map mostly to healthy-unhealthy. Pleasure or emotional happiness maps mostly to pleasant-unpleasant. Economic success maps to profit-loss. A system optimising only these three remains within the inhumane/animalistic perspective, even if it is mathematically sophisticated.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan is not saying health, pleasure, or resources are irrelevant. It is saying they are lower-order criteria. They cannot define the whole of human behaviour because humans are not merely instinctive or bodily beings. The higher criteria are justice, dharma, and truth — behaviour-relative, resolution-relative, and realisation-in-existence-relative respectively. MVD states the distinction explicitly:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “The pleasant-unpleasant perspective becomes clear with respect to instincts; healthy-unhealthy perspective becomes clear with respect to the body; profit-loss perspective becomes clear with respect to material goods and comforts; justice-injustice perspective becomes clear with respect to behaviour; dharma-adharma perspective becomes clear with respect to resolution; and truth-untruth perspective becomes clear with respect to realisation in existence.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: So the prior question is not how to optimise human systems for survival, comfort, happiness, or profit, but what a human is, what human fulfilment consists in, and which perspectives are adequate for human conduct.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1.1 Optimisation can maximise the wrong level

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: If humans optimise for survival, they may build fear-based collectives. MVD says animal collectivity appears mainly under fear, whereas awakened human sociality is based on resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “The semblance of collectivity among animals is generally observed only in situations of fear.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “The foundational basis of sociality in awakened humans is living in resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: If humans optimise for pleasure, comfort, or consumption, JV says they keep swinging between comfort-accumulation and devotion-detachment, without arriving at stable goodness:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “People enjoyed these benefits extensively, but eventually, scientific achievements also proved insufficient. Once again, humans began to feel restricted. Thus, they oscillate between devotion-detachment and comfort-accumulation…” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The argument is: maximising a partial good does not produce complete human fulfilment.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1.2 Feeling good is not the same as being good

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: JV directly rejects the idea that subjective preference can define what is good:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “Both these pursuits may feel good in themselves, but there is a distinction between ‘feeling good’ and ‘being good’. Just because something feels good doesn’t mean that it is good.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: This is a direct challenge to happiness-maximisation if happiness means felt pleasure, preference satisfaction, or emotional positivity. Madhyasth Darshan asks for a criterion beyond feeling: justice, dharma, truth, and resolution.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1.3 Parameters cannot choose themselves

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: An optimisation system needs an objective function. But the objective function is already a moral/metaphysical choice. Should society maximise:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Science can help measure and model these ends, but it cannot, by measurement alone, decide which is ultimate. Madhyasth Darshan claims the higher ordering principle is not arbitrary preference but coexistence: human conduct should be evaluated by justice, dharma, and truth in coexistence — not merely by pleasure, health, and profit.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1.4 Optimisation often becomes profit, power, and control

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: SB criticises the modern definition of development as military power, consumption, trade dominance, and accumulation:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “Nations are labelled developed if they possess the greatest military power… where the majority of people indulge in and accumulate the highest levels of food and lifestyle amenities… where most people are driven towards indulgence, over-indulgence, and excessive indulgence…” - SB

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: It then says:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “War and business, in particular, have now been reduced to ideals for all nations. However, tendencies such as war, exploitation, profit-obsession, indulgence-obsession, and sex-obsession… have not contributed to preserving the social structure or its grandeur.” - SB

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: An optimisation approach without a correct human criterion tends to optimise the measurable and controllable: wealth, power, production, consumption, military capacity, efficiency. These may increase system capability while degrading humaneness.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1.5 Human fulfilment is not a scalar variable

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan distinguishes three kinds of satisfaction:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “Sensory satisfaction proves to be momentary, intellectual satisfaction proves to be long-lasting, and spiritual satisfaction (realisation) proves to be ever-lasting or non-transformable.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: This resists collapsing fulfilment into one number called “utility” or “happiness.” A society may increase sensory satisfaction while decreasing resolution. It may increase wealth while decreasing trust. It may increase security while increasing fear. It may increase pleasure while weakening relationships.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Human order is therefore not a single-variable maximisation problem but a right-ordering problem: body needs (nourishment, protection, health), jeevan needs (values, evaluation, resolution), society needs (justice, trust, duty, prosperity, fearlessness), and existence needs (complementarity and right-use) must be kept in their proper relation.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 2.1.6 Understanding, not only behavioural tuning

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The optimization model assumes that if incentives, constraints, and metrics are correct, behaviour will become correct. Madhyasth Darshan says behaviour becomes humane only when humans understand:

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: relationships

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: values

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: justice

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: right-use

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: coexistence

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: That is why the proposed method is study leading to understanding, resolution, humane conduct, and social order — not parameter-tuning alone. This also explains the critique of power-centric governance: externally controlling behaviour cannot remove delusion.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan’s critique is strong against naive optimization — the idea that measurable survival, pleasure, productivity, or happiness can fully define human good. Metrics presuppose values; local optimisation can harm the whole; pleasure and health do not equal justice; profit and power can grow while society decays; emotional happiness can be temporary or misleading. A sophisticated scientist could respond that modern optimisation need not be crude — it can include multi-objective functions, constraints, rights, long-term ecological stability, cooperation, fairness, and preference revision. Madhyasth Darshan’s reply would be that once justice, dharma, truth, relationship-values, and coexistence enter the objective function, one is no longer doing value-neutral science alone; the real issue is what understanding of the human being supplies that function.

passages.heading: 2-can-science-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 2. Can science alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Science as an empirical method is useful and necessary for observation, production, and understanding physical processes. Scientism as a total worldview — the claim that measurable outcomes alone can settle humane ends — is insufficient. Modern science can tell us about climate damage, health, cooperation, child development, and social trust, but it does not by itself settle ultimate values. It can inform ethics; it cannot fully replace ethics. Madhyasth Darshan sometimes treats “science” as equivalent to reductionist materialism or mechanistic modernity; that is too broad. Contemporary sciences include ecology, systems theory, behavioural science, developmental psychology, and complexity studies, many of which already critique reductionism.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Religious systems often begin with the assumption that humans are sinners, ignorant, or selfish, and then prescribe rules, rituals, duties, and ideals. In Madhyasth Darshan’s reading, religion alone also cannot define correct human behaviour for that reason.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: JV states:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “All religions believe that humans are fundamentally sinners, ignorant, and selfish. However, the reality is different from this. To deliver sinners, turn the ignorant into wise, and the selfish into charitable, each religion prescribes its methods, ideals, duties, responsibilities, and rituals.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: It then asks whether this has worked:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “What has been the net outcome of these efforts? So far, there is no evidence of any ignorant person becoming wise, any selfish person becoming charitable, or any sinner being emancipated as a result of these efforts.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The alternative path is:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “The alternative path is - perform study, attain mastery, then evidence it in living.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: So Madhyasth Darshan rejects moral instruction based merely on:

passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: obedience to authority

passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: sectarian identity

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society

passages.text: scripture as unquestioned proof

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 3.1 Advaita: humans as divine

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The above critique applies most directly to religion as command, ritual, sin, sect, heaven, or scriptural authority. Advaita Vedanta is different and deserves separate treatment. It does not merely say “human is sinner.” In its strongest form, Advaita says the deepest self (Atman) is not separate from ultimate reality (Brahman). In that sense, the human is already divine at the deepest level; ignorance (avidya) hides this truth.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan recognises that Shri. Nagraj came through the Vedic/Vedantic stream and directly engaged this claim. MVD summarises the Vedantic position this way:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “According to Vedanta knowledge, only Brahma is the truth, and this world is an illusion (‘Brahma satya, jagat mithya’). However, jeeva and jagat are said to have originated from Brahma.” - MVD, The Alternative

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Shri. Nagraj’s question was:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “How can the jeeva and jagat, which originated from the Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite Brahma, be an illusion?” - MVD, The Alternative

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: SB states the Madhyasth alternative directly:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “It is presented as the postulation that ‘Brahma is truth, the world is perpetual.’” - SB, Fundamental Concepts

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The contrast is not simply Advaita saying the human is divine while Madhyasth Darshan says the human is sinful; that would be wrong. Madhyasth Darshan also gives the human a high status as a knowledge-order being capable of understanding existence, jeevan, and humane conduct. The disagreement is about what follows from that dignity. Advaita holds that the deepest self is Brahman and the world is ultimately mithya; liberation is realisation of non-duality. Madhyasth Darshan holds that existence is coexistence, the world is real and perpetual rather than illusion, and human fulfilment is evidenced through understanding, behaviour, relationships, production, right-use, justice, and universal orderliness.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: 3.2 Why Advaita is still insufficient for behaviour

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: From Madhyasth Darshan’s standpoint, saying “human is divine” is still not enough to define human behaviour unless it becomes a studiable, communicable, behavioural programme. Five limits stand out:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Divine identity does not automatically define relationship-values. If all is Brahman, what exactly is the value to be fulfilled between parent and child, spouses, teacher and student, neighbours, producer and consumer, citizen and society? Madhyasth Darshan wants these values specified and lived.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: World-as-illusion weakens the study of worldly order. If the world is ultimately mithya, then material order, biological order, family, production, ecology, and social organisation can be treated as secondary. Madhyasth Darshan instead says the world is perpetual and must be understood as coexistence.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Liberation can become inward, not social. Advaita may produce personal realisation, detachment, and equanimity. Madhyasth Darshan asks for evidence in conduct: justice, right-use, prosperity, fearlessness, family order, and undivided society.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The declaration of divinity does not by itself provide a social design — no automatic model of economy, education, governance, family, production, or ecological right-use.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: The teaching can remain ineffable. MVD contrasts mystery-based knowledge with Madhyasth Darshan’s claim that knowledge should be manifest, effable, studyable, and evidenced in behaviour:

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: “According to the idealistic scriptures and the mystery-based God-centric contemplation knowledge and tradition, the knowledge is unmanifest and ineffable. According to Madhyasth Darshan, the knowledge is manifest, effable, and understandable through studying, and its evidence becomes accessible to all through behaviour.” - MVD, The Alternative

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Unless one can answer how divine humans should behave in family, produce and use wealth, relate to nature, establish justice, organise society without domination or renunciation, and teach and verify this knowledge in conduct, the claim “human is divine” remains too abstract to define humane conduct.

passages.heading: 3-can-religion-alone-define-correct-behaviour-and-society
passages.section: 3. Can religion alone define correct behaviour and society?
passages.text: Religion often provides values, community, restraint, and discipline, but it can become dogmatic, sectarian, ritualistic, or guilt-based. Madhyasth Darshan wants ethics to be understood and evidenced, not merely obeyed. The critique may overgeneralise: many religious traditions also contain deep ethical reflection, compassion, self-discipline, service, and community care, and Advaita in particular offers a high view of human identity rather than a low view of human sinfulness. The real distinction is not religion versus Madhyasth Darshan, but that command-based or ritual-based morality is insufficient, abstract non-dual realisation is insufficient if it does not specify conduct, and understood, lived, universally verifiable humane conduct is required.

passages.heading: 4-comparing-madhyasth-darshan-science-religion-and-advaita
passages.section: 4. Comparing Madhyasth Darshan, science, religion, and Advaita
passages.text: 4. Comparing Madhyasth Darshan, science, religion, and Advaita

passages.heading: 5-practical-principles-for-behaviour
passages.text: 5. Practical principles for behaviour

passages.heading: 5-practical-principles-for-behaviour
passages.text: Ethical conduct must be based on understanding rather than blind rule-following. One should live by justice, dharma, and truth — not remain limited to pleasant-unpleasant, health-unhealth, and profit-loss. Sociality is value-fulfilment in relationships, not mere contact. Body, mind, and wealth should move from selfish use toward benevolent use. Prosperity is necessary, but hoarding and profit-obsession are disorder. Betrayal, exploitation, violence, and retaliation cannot establish orderliness. Social order requires shared cause, goal, and programme; the family is the first site of education, production, conduct, and responsibility; sectarian identity must mature into undivided society; human use of nature must become right-use rather than domination. The test of knowledge is not belief but lived proof.

passages.heading: 6-conclusion
passages.text: 6. Conclusion

passages.heading: 6-conclusion
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan offers a coherent ethical-social framework in which understanding leads to resolution, right-use, humane conduct, and undivided society. Its strength is that it refuses to separate individual conduct from social order, economy from ethics, ecology from human happiness, family from civilisation, or knowledge from behaviour.

passages.heading: 6-conclusion
passages.text: It also offers a useful critique of both dominant alternatives. Science alone can describe and optimise means, but cannot by itself define ultimate human ends. Religion alone can inspire morality, but often relies on authority, sin, ritual, and sectarian identity rather than universally studyable understanding.

passages.heading: 6-conclusion
passages.text: The most distinctive claim is that correct behaviour is neither a command from outside nor an invention by society, but the natural expression of a human who understands existence-as-coexistence, recognises jeevan, and fulfils values in relationships.

passages.heading: 6-conclusion
passages.text: Many premises depend on Shri. Nagraj’s ontology of jeevan, awakening, and coexistence. A scientist or secular ethicist may accept the practical ideals — justice, non-exploitation, ecological balance, family responsibility, and social trust — while rejecting the metaphysical foundation. A religious thinker may accept compassion and duty while questioning the rejection of scriptural authority.

passages.heading: 6-conclusion
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan is best read not merely as a moral code but as a proposed science of humane living grounded in a metaphysics of coexistence. Its social teaching asks humans to organise around understanding, relationship-values, right-use of resources, and universal orderliness. Its ethical claims are strongest as a practical critique of reductionist materialism and command-based religion; they are most debatable where they depend on the unverified ontology of jeevan and awakened realisation.
